canonical_topic: LNG as Monetization for Stranded Natural Gas Reserves
definition: A natural gas field with no pipeline connection to a major consuming region is considered 'stranded' because its gas cannot practically be sold; LNG terminals give such fields a route to market.
core_idea: Historically only a few Asian markets (Japan, South Korea, Taiwan) could receive LNG cargoes, so stranded gas had very limited outlets even if liquefied; opening North American and European markets to LNG means shipments can now enter from almost anywhere and feed into those regions' large pipeline networks, letting producers build a short pipeline to a liquefaction terminal, sign long-term overseas sales contracts, and fund further exploration.
key_points: A well with no pipeline to a major consuming market is 'stranded' — its gas can't be sold.
Historically, only Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan were realistic LNG destination markets.
Opening North American and European markets to LNG imports greatly expanded the number of viable destinations.
Producers can monetize otherwise-stranded fields by building a short pipeline to an LNG terminal and signing long-term export agreements.
relationships: Depends on global LNG terminal buildout
Follows from US LNG Terminal Reversal example
trading_implications: Long-term LNG sales agreements let low-cost producers monetize reserves that would otherwise sit undeveloped for lack of pipeline access, and the resulting cash flow can fund further exploration.
